cards.name: Atopic dermatitis (eczema)
short: A weak skin barrier lets allergens in; the immune response shifts to TH2 and IgE rises.
The hallmark symptom is itching; the look and the site change with age.
Severity is graded by SCORAD (25 and 50 are the cut-offs); status is acute, subacute or chronic.
Order of treatment: topical corticosteroid, then calcineurin inhibitor, then crisaborole, then dupilumab or tralokinumab, then a JAK inhibitor.
Basic management for every patient; on a topical steroid, seek help at 7 days and never pass 2 weeks.

steps.title: Treat it: her order of treatment
steps.q: Name the lines in order with one age limit for each, and say which steroid goes on the face.

rows: Bath: {{10 minutes}}, lukewarm, gentle non-soap cleanser, pat dry
[[occlusive|Occlusive]] moisturizer right after the bath; emollient within {{3 minutes}} while skin is damp
Avoid triggers; soft cotton clothing; lower stress
Wet wraps: short-term, {{not with calcineurin inhibitors}}
Bleach bath ({{0.005%}} sodium hypochlorite = ½ cup per full tub) {{twice a week}} for moderate–severe, to prevent repeat bacterial infection; can irritate
Non-drug care is daily; the medication is for the flare

blocks.label: First
blocks.title: [[tcs|Topical corticosteroid]]
pts: ★ First line for every severity, with basic management (her poll)
Start {{low}} potency and go up one step at a time
OTC hydrocortisone 1%: {{twice daily}} for max {{3–7 days}}
Improvement in {{24–48 hours}}
Single-ingredient products only
blocks.warn: Not resolved in 7 days: seek help. Never longer than 2 weeks.
pick: ★ {{Hydrocortisone 1%}}: "the only dose and strength that you can utilize on your face".
Not on a steroid now, even if one helped before
Start again at low potency: hydrocortisone 1% (her poll)
Low potency 1–2 times daily (face included); medium potency 1–2 times {{weekly}} (not the face)
Needs more strength from the same drug
Vehicle: {{ointment}} > cream > lotion > solution > gel > spray

blocks.label: Next
blocks.title: [[tci|Topical calcineurin inhibitor]] (second line)
pts: Twice daily; short-term and intermittent
Response in {{1–8 weeks}} (slower than a steroid) ★ she asked the room
Reassess at {{6 weeks}}
blocks.warn: Boxed warning: rare lymphoma and skin malignancy. Not under 2 years of age.
pick: Weeping lesions on wet wraps or compresses
blocks.move: Move to the next line when: the steroid and the calcineurin inhibitor have been tried.

blocks.label: Then
blocks.title: Crisaborole 2% ointment (third line)
pts: Thin layer {{twice daily}}; mild to moderate; treats flares
Used when a steroid is not appropriate, or as an adjunct
Burning and stinging
pick: Adults and children older than {{3 months}}
blocks.move: Move to the next line when: moderate to severe disease is not controlled after the topical agents.

blocks.label: Then
blocks.title: Injectable [[biologic|biologic]] (moderate to severe, after topicals)
pts: Specialty drugs; prior authorization
Dupilumab adult: {{600 mg}} once (2 × 300 mg), then {{300 mg every other week}}
May be combined with a topical corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor
Tralokinumab: the alternative to dupilumab
blocks.warn: ★ Dupilumab: no live vaccines ("I may include it on a case").
pick: {{400 mg}} once (2 × 200 mg), then {{200 mg}} every other week
600 mg once (2 × 300 mg), then 300 mg every {{4 weeks}}
Dupilumab may interact with CYP-450; doses may need adjusting
600 mg as {{four 150 mg}} injections, then 300 mg (two 150 mg) every other week; every 4 weeks if under 100 kg and clear at 16 weeks
blocks.move: Move to the next line when: disease is not controlled with other systemic or biologic therapy.

blocks.label: Last
blocks.title: JAK inhibitor (refractory)
pts: Abrocitinib and upadacitinib by mouth; ruxolitinib topical
Moderate to severe, older than {{12 years}}
Specialty follow-up every {{2 weeks}}

rows: Basic management; a flare gets a low-to-medium potency steroid
Maintenance steroid, OR calcineurin inhibitor, OR crisaborole 2% twice daily
Systemic immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, methotrexate, mycophenolate, azathioprine: not FDA-approved for this)
Systemic corticosteroids: not for long-term maintenance
Consider nonadherence, infection, misdiagnosis, contact allergy to the medication; refer
Anti-inflammatory activity rises with a C1–C2 double bond, a 6α or 9α halogen and an 11β-OH (DPAW page 20)
Similar in lipophilicity, structure and mechanism; pimecrolimus binds skin protein more (few systemic adverse effects), tacrolimus less (DPAW page 28)

patients.t: A 21-year-old man has itching behind the knees and inside the elbows. The skin is dry and inflamed, with no infection and no lichenified plaques. SCORAD is 40.
patients.q: How do you describe the severity and status?
o: Mild, acute
Moderate, acute
Moderate, subacute
Severe, chronic
patients.w: SCORAD 25–50 is moderate; dry, inflamed lesions without lichenification are subacute. This is her poll patient (slides 23–24, 49).

x.Mild, acute: SCORAD 40 is above 25, and acute lesions have vesicles, exudate and crusts with no dryness.
x.Moderate, acute: The score fits, but dry inflamed skin without vesicles or exudate is subacute.
x.Severe, chronic: Severe is above 50, and chronic needs lichenified plaques, which he does not have.

patients.t: The same 21-year-old was diagnosed at age 10. Corticosteroids helped in the past, but he uses none now. He takes loratadine for allergic rhinitis.
patients.q: Which prescription fits first-line maintenance for him?
o: Hydrocortisone 1%, thin layer twice daily for 3–7 days
Mometasone furoate 0.1%, thin layer once daily for 3–7 days
Pimecrolimus 1% cream, thin layer twice daily for 6 weeks
Triamcinolone 0.1%, thick layer twice daily for 3–7 days

x.Triamcinolone 0.1%, thick layer twice da: Medium potency is not the starting step, and the layer is thin, not thick.

patients.t: An 18-month-old has mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis on the arms and legs. Hydrocortisone 1% used correctly gave no response. The parents ask what comes next.
o: Pimecrolimus 1% cream twice daily
Tacrolimus 0.03% ointment twice daily
Crisaborole 2% ointment twice daily
Dupilumab 300 mg every 4 weeks

x.Pimecrolimus 1% cream twice daily: Second line by order, but not for children under 2 years.
x.Tacrolimus 0.03% ointment twice daily: The 0.03% strength is for ages 2 to 15; under 2 it is not recommended.
x.Dupilumab 300 mg every 4 weeks: Injectables are for moderate-to-severe disease after the topical agents.

patients.t: An adult is prescribed triamcinolone 0.1% cream to both arms, hands included, twice daily for 5 days.
patients.w: One arm with the hand is 4 units, so two arms are 8 units = 4 g per application. 4 g × 2 × 5 = 40 g, rounded up to 45 g (slides 10–11, 13).

x.60 g: Larger than needed; 40 g rounds up to the next size, which is 45 g.

o: 600 mg once, then 300 mg every other week
400 mg once, then 200 mg every other week

patients.t: A 30-year-old has used OTC hydrocortisone 1% twice daily on her forearms for 8 days. The patches are no better, and one now has yellow crusts and pus.
o: Continue hydrocortisone 1% to day 14, then reassess

x.Change to an OTC petrolatum ointment and: A moisturizer is part of basic management but does not address a possible infection.

cards.name: Diaper dermatitis
short: Occlusion, moisture and friction under the diaper, with enzymes, bile salts and an alkaline skin pH.
Red to bright red, shiny, wet-looking patches in the diaper area; no lichenification.
Refer for lesions over 7 days, signs of infection, broken skin, rash outside the diaper area, or fever.
Treat with ABCDE and a skin protectant: zinc oxide in a petrolatum base at every change.
No hydrocortisone, antifungal, antibacterial or anesthetic as self-care; follow up at 7 days.

x.Stop the protectant and use air drying o: Barrier is one of the five ABCDE steps and continues.

cards.name: Acne
short: Androgens raise sebum; keratin plugs the follicle; P. acnes grows; inflammation follows.
Lesions: comedones (non-inflammatory), then papules, pustules, nodules or cysts (inflammatory).
Her grades use the words rare, some, many and no more than one nodule.
One agent, then two, then three; topical before oral; benzoyl peroxide first.
Visible benefit takes 8 weeks or more; isotretinoin needs iPledge.

atopic-march: The typical progression of allergic diseases that begin early in life: allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic dermatitis and food allergies.
flg: FLG encodes profilaggrin, which degrades to filaggrins; they form the skin barrier, and their breakdown products are natural moisturizers.
tewl: Trans-epidermal water loss; reducing it is a treatment goal.
tci: Topical calcineurin inhibitor: pimecrolimus or tacrolimus.
pde4: Phosphodiesterase 4, the enzyme that breaks down cAMP in inflammatory cells; crisaborole inhibits it.

skin-protectant: A product such as zinc oxide, petrolatum, calamine or cocoa butter that gives the skin a physical barrier and lubrication and reduces irritation.
Patel Dermatitis slide 63; Outdoor slide 39; Sun slide 31
comedone: A plugged follicle, non-inflammatory: open = blackhead, closed = whitehead.
papule: A small, raised, solid bump on the skin. In acne (Dr. Patel): an inflammatory lesion, raised and red, with no visible pus.
Patel Acne slides 5–6; 11/10 lecture; the first sentence is the plain meaning
pustule: An inflammatory lesion with visible white pus.
nodule: A large inflammatory lesion under the skin; the worst stage of acne. A foreign body response to the papule; it does not drain (Dr. Smith).

keratolytic: Thins the skin on and around the lesion, so the outer layer loosens and sheds; softens keratin. Benzoyl peroxide, sulfur, salicylic acid and the alpha hydroxy acids are keratolytics.

comedolytic: Lyses comedones and prevents new ones; loosens the plug of cells and oil.
ipledge: The FDA-regulated program (a REMS) for isotretinoin, a potent teratogen: registration, consent, pregnancy tests and limited fill windows.
pcos: Polycystic ovary syndrome (plain meaning, not from the slides); her slide names it as the exception for endocrine testing.
bp: Benzoyl peroxide, in the key of her algorithm slide.
hygiene: The absence of early childhood exposure to infectious agents increases susceptibility to allergic diseases. Dr. Smith’s slide gives it with the lower prevalence in rural areas.
fkbp: The protein that tacrolimus (FK506) binds inside the T cell; the tacrolimus–FKBP complex inactivates calcineurin.
jak: An enzyme. A JAK inhibitor blocks it, so fewer inflammatory cytokines are produced (Dr. Smith) and the downstream immune-mediated inflammatory response decreases (Dr. Patel).
Smith PCol slides 75–76; Patel Dermatitis slide 46

pairs.title: Pimecrolimus or tacrolimus?
a: 1% cream; mild to moderate; older than 2 years and adults
b: Ointment; moderate to severe; 0.1% older than 16 years, 0.03% from 2 to 15 years
pairs.same: Topical calcineurin inhibitors: second line for atopic dermatitis, twice daily, response in 1–8 weeks, not under 2 years, boxed warning for rare lymphoma and skin malignancy.
profs: "Understand the difference between the two": severity, dosage form, strength and age (Patel Dermatitis slide 39).
Tacrolimus binds FKBP and the complex inhibits calcineurin; pimecrolimus is listed as a calcineurin inhibitor (PCol slides 24–27).
Pimecrolimus cLogP 6.0 with high skin protein binding, so few systemic effects; tacrolimus cLogP 5.8 with low skin protein binding, so more systemic entry (DPAW pages 28, 32).

pairs.title: Two PDE-4 inhibitors: crisaborole or apremilast?
pairs.same: Both inhibit phosphodiesterase 4, so cAMP is not broken down and inflammatory cells are inhibited.
profs: PDE-4 inhibitors: crisaborole for atopic dermatitis, apremilast for psoriasis (PCol slides 32–34).
Crisaborole: a benzoxaborole whose boron coordinates Zn2+ and Mg2+ in the PDE4 site (DPAW pages 7, 9). Apremilast: an isoindoline, CYP3A4 substrate; avoid 3A4 inhibitors and inducers (DPAW page 34).
Crisaborole: third line, mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis, from 3 months of age (Patel Dermatitis slides 41–42).

pairs.title: Dupilumab or tralokinumab: which target?
a: Binds the IL-4 receptor α subunit, blocking IL-4 and IL-13 signaling; two 300 mg injections to load
b: Inhibits the IL-13 cytokine; four 150 mg injections to load
pairs.same: Subcutaneous biologics for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis after topical therapy; maintenance every other week.
profs: Dupilumab binds IL-4Rα, shared by the IL-4 and IL-13 receptor complexes (PCol slide 64). Tralokinumab is not on her slides.
Her slide titles dupilumab an IL-4 antagonist (slide 43) and tralokinumab an IL-13 cytokine inhibitor, the alternative to dupilumab (slide 45).

pairs.title: Mometasone 0.1%: ointment or cream?
pairs.same: The same drug at the same strength; the vehicle changes the potency. Ointment > cream > lotion > solution > gel > spray.
profs: "Highlight that, please, so you understand that there is a difference there" (Patel Dermatitis slide 37; 11/06 lecture).
Changing the vehicle, hydration or occlusion may alter absorption and effectiveness (PCol slide 11).

pairs.title: Topical retinoids: adapalene, tretinoin or tazarotene?
b: Prescription only; tazarotene is an ester prodrug
pairs.same: Topical retinoids acting at RAR/RXR: keratolytic and comedolytic, not bactericidal; applied in the evening with sunscreen by day.
profs: Adapalene 0.1% gel became OTC in 2016; at night, apart from benzoyl peroxide. Prescription retinoids: tretinoin, tazarotene, trifarotene (Patel Acne slides 27, 31).
Tretinoin, adapalene and tazarotene bind RAR and RXR (PCol slides 14, 17–18, 20).

Tretinoin: first generation, all-trans retinoic acid. Adapalene: third generation, exposed COOH, directly active. Tazarotene: third generation, ethyl ester prodrug to tazarotenic acid (DPAW pages 29, 49, 51).

pairs.title: Oral tetracyclines: doxycycline and minocycline, or sarecycline?
a: 50–100 mg twice daily or 100 mg daily; the most prescribed
b: Once daily by weight band (60, 100 or 150 mg); non-nodular moderate to severe acne
pairs.same: Tetracyclines that bind the 30S ribosomal subunit; photosensitivity; avoided in pregnancy; with a topical combination, never as the only therapy.
profs: Tetracyclines only above 12 years (tooth discoloration); re-evaluate at 3–4 months (Patel Acne slide 33; 11/10 lecture).
Sarecycline, minocycline and doxycycline block aminoacyl-tRNA binding at the 30S acceptor site (PCol slide 43).
Doxycycline and minocycline are lipophilic and food does not cut their absorption, unlike tetracycline with dairy (DPAW page 55).
